topics.topic: Access-version preconditions and stale-version behavior for session-access mutations
questions: Which session-access mutations are conditional on the access version, and what happens on a stale version?
Which session-access mutations require an expected access version, and what happens on a stale version?
What changes the access version, and must grant, revoke, active-project change, request replacement and request answer state the version they were made against?

quotes: the session's granted project ids, its active project if any, whether it has a pending request, and the access version — no `personal_data` value (R0-32, R0-46, R0-64)
A change states the revision it was made against; a change against an older revision is refused and nothing changes. Every change is atomic.
judgement.why: Mutation preconditions, version-transition rules and stale-input behavior are rules and required tests owned by State 2.

topics.topic: Behavior and revision effects of repeated customer restriction transitions
questions: Are repeated restrict and lift requests idempotent, or are they refused?
What is the observable result of restricting an already restricted customer or lifting a restriction that is not present, and do these no-op requests move the customer revision?
What happens when the owner restricts an already restricted customer or lifts a restriction that is not present?

quotes: the Customer marked restricted, or no longer restricted where a lawful ground allows it; while restricted, its contact data stays stored and reaches no one but the owner, no project may newly name it, and every other use of its contact data is refused — Registry admits no exception; where a lawful ground allows processing, the owner lifts the restriction (R0-65); corrections of its existing projects that do not use that data go on, and `context` keeps its `customer_ref` (R0-37, R0-51, R0-55)

A project, a customer and an object carry a revision that every accepted change moves. A change states the revision it was made against; a change against an older revision is refused and nothing changes. Every change is atomic.
judgement.why: Idempotency, refusal and revision effects for repeated state transitions are operational rules owned by State 2.

topics.topic: Behavior when answering an access request with an ineligible or already granted project
questions: Does answering a request by granting an unknown, archived or already granted project fail, clear the request, or apply the ordinary grant rules?
What happens if the selected project is unknown, archived, anonymised, deleted, or already granted when the owner answers the request?
What happens if the selected project is unknown, archived, anonymised, deleted or already granted when the owner answers the request?

quotes: either answer clears the pending request; granting adds the project the owner picks from the catalogue to the session's set (and, if asked, makes it active); declining leaves the set unchanged and keeps no reason; the session reads the outcome in its access (R0-46, R0-47, R0-64)
unknown or archived project refused; unknown session refused
judgement.why: The eligibility checks, set-insertion semantics and atomic effect of answering a request are rules and required tests owned by State 2.

topics.topic: Exact coverage of actions and state changes written to the audit log
questions: Exactly which primary actions create audit entries?

Exactly which state-changing actions are audited: room additions, artifact publication and withdrawal, session registration, active-project changes, access requests and answers, imports, archives, and refused attempts?

Exactly which new actions are significant and audited—for example room creation, artifact publication or withdrawal, session registration, active-project changes, access requests and answers, imports, relationship end or resume, and audit-log erasure?

judgement.why: This is the same question as P1 about the exact accepted and refused actions that create audit entries, and the relevant passages have not changed.

precedent.topic: Accepted and refused actions that must create audit entries
quotes:
Registry records only significant changes of state: changes to projects and
customer records, granting and revoking an agent session's projects,
restricting processing and lifting it, and erasures and anonymisations. Ordinary reads, agent calls and the inner steps of flows
are not recorded in Registry; security events of the infrastructure are
handled by the infrastructure, outside Registry.

- **Audit.** A minimal log of significant changes of state (R0-58): time, the
  acting principal (owner, which service, agent through Kernel), the change,
  the project or customer, the outcome, the contract and release version, and
  a confirmation id where the owner confirmed.
precedent.why: The exact event-selection and outcome-recording criteria are operational rules and required tests owned by State 2.

topics.topic: Guarantee that agent-visible outputs and free-form references contain no personal data
questions: How does Registry guarantee that artifact-pointer data returned to an agent contains no `personal_data` value?
What guarantees that project and room names or artifact-pointer values exposed to an agent contain no personal data?
What concrete output filtering or disclosure guarantee does K-14 provide, given that K-14 is not defined in this text?
How is the no-personal-values guarantee preserved when agent-visible display names, room names, artifact URIs, payload references or digests can themselves contain identifying information?

quotes: It holds no owner credential and no Registry service token, never receives a `personal_data` value (R0-26), and has no administrative access to the production host, its store, configuration, secrets or deployment (R0-25).
the minimal projection of that project: its id, display name, status, rooms and artifact pointers — no address, customer or other personal value
A pointer carries `uri`, `payload_ref` or both; one with neither is refused.
A pointer may carry a content digest of the artifact; Registry stores it and never computes or checks it against the payload.

Registry publishes its operations through the platform manifest (`platform/manifest/registry.json`); the agent studies them, proposes operation bindings, writes pure functions and runs flows in Kernel, and receives only what K-14 lets through.
judgement.divergence: One implementation validates, rejects or redacts identifying project names, room names, URIs, payload references and digests before an agent can receive them; another accepts those caller-supplied values and returns them unchanged, which the producer notices through rejection or alteration and the agent notices in its visible output.
judgement.why: The unconditional no-personal-data promise covers agent-visible values, but the texts neither name an enforcement action or failure nor expose the undefined K-14 guarantee as an open question.

What happens when the owner ends an already ended relationship, resumes one that is not ended, or supplies a different end date for an already ended relationship?

quotes: the Customer marked as ended on that date, or the mark cleared; archiving its projects does not end it (R0-49, R0-57, R0-60)
The end of a relationship with a customer is recorded by the owner, by an explicit action; archiving the customer's projects does not end it.
judgement.why: The source and replacement rules for the date and the behavior of repeated transitions are operational rules and required tests owned by State 2.

topics.topic: Audit target identifiers and their compatibility with the no-personal-data rule
questions: Must an audit entry for a grant or revocation identify the agent session as well as the project?

How can an audit entry identify the affected project or customer while carrying no personal value, when a project identity is explicitly not anonymous by itself and a customer reference may identify a person?

quotes: - **Audit.** A minimal log of significant changes of state (R0-58): time, the acting principal (owner, which service, agent through Kernel), the change, the project or customer, the outcome, the contract and release version, and a confirmation id where the owner confirmed.
No personal value, whole request or secret enters it.
a project's id is not anonymous by itself and is never `open` merely for being an id.
judgement.why: The identifiers and fields carried by each audit-entry variant, including a session identifier, are model and schema questions owned by State 1.

topics.topic: Behavior of repeated session grants and repeated active-project selection
questions: What happens when the owner grants a project the session already has?
What happens when the project is already granted, is already active, or is granted again with a request to make it active?

quotes: the project joins the session's granted set; the owner may also make it the session's active project (R0-46)
Registry keeps for each session the set of granted `project_id`s and at most one active project, the default when the agent names none.
judgement.why: Set idempotency and repeated active-selection effects are operational rules and required tests owned by State 2.

topics.topic: Result of an agent project operation with neither project ID nor active project
questions: What observable result occurs when an agent-authority operation omits `project_id` and the session has no active project?
What happens when an agent-authority project operation supplies no project id and the session has no active project?

quotes: Registry keeps for each session the set of granted `project_id`s and at most one active project, the default when the agent names none.
judgement.divergence: One implementation refuses the operation because no project was named or active; another selects a granted project or otherwise proceeds, and Cabinet Kernel and the agent notice whether the requested project operation fails or acts on a project.
judgement.why: The defaulting promise has no defined observable output or failure for the permitted state in which the session has no active project.

topics.topic: Revision preconditions for owner-interface mutations across record and non-record state
questions: Which owner-interface changes are revision-conditional: only project and customer record changes, or also archive, restriction, relationship, session access, artifact and audit changes?
Which owner changes require which revision, given that only projects and customers have record revisions while session access, imports and the audit log also have owner changes?

quotes: Every change carries CSRF protection and is validated on the server; a change made against an older revision is refused (R0-35).

A project, a customer and an object carry a revision that every accepted change moves. A change states the revision it was made against; a change against an older revision is refused and nothing changes. Every change is atomic.
Narrowed by R0-45: the object has no revision of its own; a change of it moves the project's.
judgement.why: Mapping revision preconditions to individual mutations and defining their stale-input tests are State 2 rules.

topics.topic: Rules for clearing or selecting the active project, including archived projects
questions: Which action clears a session's active project, and what does it return or refuse?
Does this action explicitly allow clearing the active project, and may an archived but still granted project be selected as active?

quotes: Changing the active project revokes nothing; the owner may also clear it, and revoking the active project clears it (round 6 T10).

the session's active project changes, which revokes nothing; or the project leaves the session's set, and every later operation on it in that session — a running flow's next step included — is refused (R0-46)
Archiving a project keeps it in a set but refuses agent writes on it (R0-12).
judgement.divergence: One implementation accepts an explicit clear and permits any granted archived project to become active; another lacks a clear input or refuses archived selection, and the owner notices the resulting active project while Kernel and the agent notice which project is used by default.
judgement.why: Although clearing is promised, its action result and failures are not stated, and the texts leave archived-project selection observably open.

quotes: The sections above the decisions describe the frame as it stands after them.
The answers to question round 18 were proposed to the owner and accepted on 2026-10-27 (R0-61 to R0-67).

topics.topic: Whether and how an anonymised project can be anonymised again or deleted whole
questions: May an anonymised project later be deleted whole, and what happens if anonymisation is requested again?

May an anonymised project later be erased again and deleted whole, and if so how can the owner select it through the owner interface when project reads only answer that it was erased and lists omit it?

quotes: the project anonymised — its id, status and artifact pointers stay, its name, object and customer link go, `validate` answers `archived` — or deleted whole, `validate` answering `not_found`; the owner chooses (R0-60); either way it leaves every agent session's set and is active in none (R0-61)

An anonymised project keeps its id, status and artifact pointers and nothing else. `validate` answers `archived`, and its artifacts are listed and read as before. 'Read a project', `context` and the agent projection answer that it was erased, and 'list projects' never lists it.
The owner interface carries every action whose 'who' names the owner.
judgement.divergence: One implementation lets the owner address an anonymised project by id, treats repeated anonymisation as unchanged and permits later whole deletion; another refuses any further erase because the project was already erased or provides no way to select it, and the owner notices whether the retained record can be removed.
judgement.why: The retained record remains archived and therefore appears eligible for the erase action, but the texts give no repeated-erasure behavior or owner-interface path for selecting it.
